memory_update.text: AI infrastructure supply chain should be tracked as a relay of constraints: accelerators/HBM -> advanced packaging/test -> networking optics/photonics -> rack power/liquid cooling -> grid interconnection/power availability -> automation software.
HBM interface IP, memory-controller validation, and HBM test are underfollowed nodes adjacent to the obvious HBM manufacturer trade.
Advanced packaging tools, substrates, bonding, inspection, and burn-in/test should be prioritized as possible AI accelerator chokepoints beyond TSMC capacity headlines.
AI optics/photonics discovery should include InP substrates, silicon photonics, external light sources, CW lasers, module components, and photonics test rather than only switch vendors.

Liquid-cooling and rack-power discovery should search outside obvious data-center infrastructure leaders for component suppliers in cold plates, CDUs, pumps, valves, sensors, busway, PDUs, and controls.
Grid interconnection, transformers, switchgear, substations, and transmission services may become limiting constraints for AI data-center deployment and should be mapped to public suppliers.
Layer 1B should run focused primary-source searches for each node, build a 20+ company candidate universe, and separate reference leaders from underfollowed small/mid-cap suppliers.

layer1a.summary: Layer 1A decomposes AI infrastructure as a constraint-relay system rather than a single GPU trade. The broad demand wave begins with hyperscaler and enterprise AI capex, but investable bottlenecks may migrate across HBM, advanced packaging, optics/photonics, power/cooling, grid interconnection, and automation software. For Serenity-style discovery, reference leaders such as NVIDIA, TSMC, Broadcom, Arista, Vertiv, Eaton, and hyperscalers define the architecture, while the higher-value research lane is likely in less-followed suppliers one or two steps upstream: HBM interface/IP, packaging tools and test, InP/photonics substrates and lasers, liquid-cooling components, transformers/switchgear, grid construction, interconnection services, and data-center automation. This is research support only; no buy/sell view is implied.

demand_drivers: Hyperscaler AI training and inference clusters requiring accelerators, HBM, high-speed networking, power delivery, cooling, and new data-center capacity.
Custom AI ASIC adoption by cloud platforms and large model operators, increasing demand for advanced packaging, HBM, Ethernet/optical fabrics, and verification/test infrastructure.
Rising accelerator rack power density, pushing data centers toward liquid cooling, upgraded power distribution, backup power, switchgear, and thermal management.
Grid connection delays and electricity availability becoming constraints on where AI data centers can be sited and how quickly they can come online.

Architecture shifts toward co-packaged optics, silicon photonics, external light sources, and higher-speed optical interconnects as electrical networking reaches distance, power, and bandwidth limits.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Start from the system architecture: AI compute cluster -> accelerator and memory -> package/test -> network fabric and optics -> rack power and liquid cooling -> building electrical systems -> utility/grid interconnection -> automation/orchestration software. Use reference leaders to map demand and standards, then deliberately search for public companies with narrow exposure to required components, tools, certifications, IP, materials, or services. Favor evidence from filings, earnings calls, customer certifications, capacity expansions, standards participation, patents, and capex commentary. Social-media or Serenity-style references are usable only as leads, not proof.
supply_side_constraints: HBM capacity is structurally tied to DRAM conversion, stack yield, packaging availability, and customer qualification cycles.
Advanced packaging capacity, especially 2.5D/3D integration such as CoWoS-like flows and hybrid bonding, can bottleneck completed accelerator supply even when GPU dies and memory exist.
Optical communication supply chains may be constrained by niche substrates, lasers, photonic devices, test equipment, and qualification bottlenecks.
Power infrastructure constraints include transformers, switchgear, substations, turbines, transmission construction, and interconnection queues.
Thermal infrastructure constraints include CDU systems, cold plates, pumps, valves, dielectric fluids, leak detection, and data-center integration expertise.
